Frankly
frăŋk´lī
adv. (freely, without charge or condition; of a creditor forgiving two debtors)
From Old French franc, free — the Franks being the free people of their territory. Luke's Greek is charizomai, from charis, grace: to forgive as a free gift. Frankly in 1611 means freely, not candidly.

Biblical Definition

Christ, dining with a Pharisee who is scandalized by the woman washing His feet, answers with a parable about arithmetic: “There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty” (Luke 7:41). Then the point on which everything turns: “And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?” (Luke 7:42). Frankly is freely — the debt was not reduced, rescheduled, or partly worked off. Both debtors had nothing, and both were released outright. Simon answers correctly that the one forgiven most will love most, and Christ applies it: “Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little” (Luke 7:47). The woman's love is the evidence of a forgiveness already received, not its purchase price — the parable Christ has just told makes the order unmistakable, since the creditor forgave before either debtor felt anything. And the danger in the room was never the woman's: “For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself” (Galatians 6:3). Simon owed fifty and thought he owed nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines frankly as without reserve, constraint or disguise; liberally; freely; readily — and cites the Scripture sense of freely giving.

expand to see more

FRANKLY, adv. Openly; freely; ingenuously; without reserve, constraint or disguise.

FRANKLY, adv. Liberally; freely; readily; as, he frankly forgave them both.

FRANK, a. [Fr. franc, free.] Open; ingenuous; candid; free in uttering real sentiments; liberal; generous.

FORGIVE, v.t. To pardon; to remit, as an offense or debt; to overlook an offense, and treat the offender as not guilty.

CREDITOR, n. [L. creditor.] A person to whom a sum of money or other thing is due, by borrowing or purchase.

Key Scripture

Luke 7:41 — "There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty."

Luke 7:42 — "And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?"

Luke 7:47 — "Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little."

Galatians 6:3 — "For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself."

Modern Corruption

Verse 47 is read as though the woman's love purchased her forgiveness, reversing the order the parable in verses 41 and 42 was told to establish.

expand to see more

Her sins…are forgiven; for she loved much looks, in isolation, like love earning pardon, and it has been read that way in defence of a merit-based scheme. The parable Christ has just told forbids it. The creditor forgave both debtors when they had nothing to pay, before any love was shown, and the question He put to Simon was which of them will love him most — a future consequence of a past release. The for of verse 47 is evidential, not causal: her love proves the forgiveness, as the Greek construction and the whole shape of the story require. The last clause of the verse confirms it, since a man who loves little is described as one to whom little is forgiven.

The other half of the passage is aimed at the host, and it is the half that a respectable congregation should feel. Simon is the fifty-pence debtor, and his problem is that he thinks the figure is zero. He has given Christ no water, no kiss, no oil — ordinary courtesies — while a woman off the street has not ceased to kiss His feet. Little forgiven, little loved. The coldness of a settled and well-behaved Christian is very often exactly this: not a want of feeling but a want of any estimate of the debt.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek charizomai (G5483), to give freely, forgive; charis (G5485), grace; daneistes (G1157), a creditor; chreopheiletes (G5533), a debtor.

expand to see more

Greek charizomai (G5483) — to forgive as a free gift; Luke 7:42, rendered frankly forgave.

Greek charis (G5485) — grace; the root of the verb, and the whole of the parable.

Greek daneistes (G1157) — a moneylender, creditor; only Luke 7:41.

Greek chreopheiletes (G5533) — a debtor; both men, at different sums.

Greek hoti (G3754) — for, because; evidential in verse 47, as the parable requires.

Usage

"“When they had nothing to pay” — the condition of both debtors."

"“He frankly forgave them both” — freely, and before any love appeared."

"“To whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little” — and Simon is the fifty."
